question: Why is the cabin pressurised?

options.text: So that the packs can operate at high altitude
So that the cabin air is cooler
So that occupants experience a much lower cabin altitude than the aircraft's real altitude
So that the fuselage skin is not stressed in flight

explanation: A pressurised cabin keeps the occupants at an altitude where oxygen is available in adequate quantity. The skin is in fact stressed by the pressure difference, which is why the differential pressure is limited.

question: What is meant by differential pressure (ΔP)?

options.text: The cabin pressure minus the outside ambient pressure
The pressure drop across the outflow valve
The difference between pack 1 and pack 2 outlet pressure
The difference between the QNH and the QFE

explanation: ΔP is what loads the fuselage structure. The system controls cabin altitude and rate of change so that ΔP remains inside structural limits.

question: How many cabin pressure controllers (CPCs) are installed, and how do they operate?

options.text: One for each pack, both active together
Three, in a voting arrangement
One in the cockpit and one in the cargo hold, working in parallel
Two; one controls at a time and the other is in standby, and they swap roles after each flight

explanation: Only one CPC is active, and the roles alternate on each landing so both are exercised. If the active one fails, the standby takes over automatically.

question: What happens when the active cabin pressure controller fails?

options.text: The outflow valve closes to hold the current pressure
The other controller takes over automatically
The cabin immediately depressurises
The crew must switch to manual at once

explanation: The system is built to remain automatic after one failure. Only a failure of both controllers sends the crew to manual mode.

question: How many outflow valves does the A320 have, and how are they driven?

options.text: Two outflow valves, one forward and one aft, driven by hydraulic jacks
One outflow valve, driven by one of three electric motors: two automatic and one manual
One outflow valve driven only by the pneumatic system
Three outflow valves, one per cabin zone

explanation: The two automatic motors are used by the CPCs; the manual motor is used when the MODE SEL is set to MAN, via the MAN V/S CTL switch.

question: Where is the outflow valve located?

options.text: In the cockpit ceiling
On the forward cargo door
In the left wing root
On the lower rear fuselage, near the aft pressure bulkhead

explanation: It discharges cabin air overboard in the aft underside of the fuselage, which also gives a small thrust benefit as the air leaves.

question: What controls the outflow valve in normal operation?

options.text: One of the cabin pressure controllers, using the automatic motors
The pilot, via the MAN V/S CTL switch
The position of the pack flow selector
The differential pressure alone, through a mechanical bellows

explanation: The CPC drives the outflow valve to follow the pressurisation schedule it computes from flight data.

question: Which data does the cabin pressure controller use to compute the pressurisation schedule in automatic mode?

options.text: The cabin temperature and the passenger count
The engine N1 and the flap position only
Landing elevation, destination QNH and cruise altitude from the FMGS, plus aircraft altitude and air/ground status
The weather radar returns

explanation: The system anticipates the descent: it needs to know where it is going (destination elevation and pressure) and how high it will cruise so that cabin altitude can follow a smooth schedule.

question: What does the LDG ELEV selector do in AUTO?

options.text: The cabin altitude is set to sea level
The outflow valve is held fully open
The cabin altitude warning is inhibited
The landing elevation is taken automatically from the FMGS destination data

explanation: If the FMGS data are unavailable, the crew sets the landing elevation manually with the selector, so the CPC can still plan the descent.

question: What is the range of the manually selectable landing elevation on the LDG ELEV selector?

options.text: From 0 to 10 000 ft
From about –2 000 ft to about 14 000 ft
From –1 000 ft to 8 000 ft
From sea level to 20 000 ft

explanation: The range covers any airport a transport aircraft will use. The selected value is displayed on the PRESS page.

question: What does setting the MODE SEL to MAN do?

options.text: It switches the active CPC to the standby one
It closes the safety valves
It disables the automatic CPC control and gives the crew control of the outflow valve through the MAN V/S CTL switch
It opens the outflow valve fully

explanation: In manual mode the crew controls the vertical speed of the cabin altitude (up or down), and must manage the cabin altitude and ΔP by monitoring the ECAM.

question: With the MODE SEL in MAN, what does moving the MAN V/S CTL switch to UP do?

options.text: It drives the outflow valve towards open, increasing cabin altitude
It drives the outflow valve towards closed, decreasing cabin altitude
It increases the pack flow
It raises the landing elevation setting

explanation: UP means up with the cabin altitude, which is the outflow valve opening and the cabin pressure falling. DN closes the valve so the cabin pressure rises.

question: Why is the outflow valve driven to open fully shortly after landing?

options.text: So the cabin is fully depressurised and the doors can be opened safely
To cool the cargo hold
To start the avionics ventilation
To allow the packs to restart

explanation: After touchdown the CPC drives the valve open and the cabin ΔP is brought to zero, which also matters for door safety.

question: What is pre-pressurisation, and when is it done?

options.text: A test of the cabin pressure controller at engine start
A pressurisation of the cargo hold before loading
A small cabin pressure increase on the ground before take-off, so that rotation does not cause a pressure bump
A reduction of the cabin pressure during taxi

explanation: On take-off the cabin altitude is first driven slightly below the airfield elevation, which avoids a sudden pressure change when the aircraft rotates and the thrust changes.

question: Which statement describes the cabin altitude during the climb in automatic mode?

options.text: It increases as quickly as the aircraft climbs
It increases gradually at a controlled rate, following a schedule that depends on the aircraft altitude
It stays at sea level until cruise altitude
It follows the ΔP limit only

explanation: The CPC limits the cabin rate of climb so passengers are comfortable, and the cabin altitude in cruise is kept well below the aircraft altitude.

question: During the descent in automatic mode, what determines the cabin altitude the system aims for at landing?

options.text: Always sea level
The highest altitude of the flight
The elevation of the departure airport
The landing field elevation, so that the cabin pressure equals the field pressure on touchdown

explanation: The CPC wants the cabin pressure to equal the outside pressure at touchdown, so the outflow valve can open and the doors can open without a pressure difference.

question: What is the purpose of the two safety valves?

options.text: To regulate the cabin altitude in normal flight
To drain water from the cabin
To prevent excessive positive differential pressure and to provide a negative relief function, as a back-up to the outflow valve
To control the cabin temperature

explanation: The safety valves are not normally used for control. They open mechanically if the cabin ΔP gets too high or negative.

question: At what differential pressure do the safety valves open, approximately?

options.text: About 8.6 psi
About 5 psi
About 12 psi
About 3 psi

explanation: The normal maximum ΔP is about 8.06 psi; the safety valves lie just above it, to open only when the normal control has failed.

question: What is the approximate maximum normal differential pressure of the A320 family in automatic control?

options.text: About 4 psi
About 12 psi
About 15 psi
About 8 psi (8.06 psi)

explanation: Cabin ΔP is a structural limit: the fuselage is designed to carry it, and the system keeps the cabin altitude as low as that limit allows at the maximum operating altitude.

question: What does the negative pressure relief protect against?

options.text: Too high a cabin temperature
A situation where the outside pressure is higher than the cabin pressure, for example in a rapid descent without enough outflow
Overpressure in the pneumatic duct
Electrical overload of the outflow valve motors

explanation: A negative ΔP loads the structure in the opposite direction. The safety valves are arranged to open inward, so that the cabin pressure never falls too far below ambient.

question: At approximately what cabin altitude is the CAB PR EXCESS CAB ALT warning triggered?

options.text: About 5 000 ft
About 9 550 ft
About 12 000 ft
About 14 000 ft

explanation: Above this altitude the ECAM tells the crew that the cabin altitude is excessive. A further rise to 14 000 ft causes the passenger oxygen masks to deploy.

question: At approximately what cabin altitude do the passenger oxygen masks drop automatically?

options.text: About 8 000 ft
About 10 000 ft
About 20 000 ft
About 14 000 ft

explanation: The masks present automatically at around 14 000 ft cabin altitude. The cockpit crew must use their own oxygen masks as soon as the warning appears.

question: What does the PRESS page of the ECAM show?

options.text: Cabin altitude, cabin vertical speed, differential pressure, outflow valve position, safety valve position and the CPC in control
The pack flow and bleed temperatures
The hydraulic pressure of each system
The oxygen bottle pressure

explanation: It is the page to watch for any pressurisation fault, and it is displayed automatically when an advisory or fault occurs in the system.

question: What happens when both CPCs have failed?

options.text: The system keeps working in a degraded automatic mode
The outflow valve closes and stays closed
A CAB PR SYS 1+2 FAULT message appears and the crew must control the outflow valve manually
The packs shut down

explanation: The manual motor and the MAN V/S CTL switch remain available, so the crew can maintain a comfortable cabin altitude manually.

question: In manual pressurisation mode, who is responsible for avoiding exceeding the maximum cabin ΔP?

options.text: The CPC, which still limits ΔP in the background
The packs, which reduce flow automatically
Nobody, because the safety valves take over
The crew, by monitoring the cabin altitude, ΔP and V/S on the ECAM

explanation: The safety valves remain as a last resort, but should not be used for control. In manual mode the crew has to manage everything.

question: Which procedure follows a cabin altitude excess warning if the cabin cannot be controlled?

options.text: Selecting the packs to HI flow and continuing
Crew oxygen masks on, then an emergency descent to a safe altitude
Selecting the RAM AIR pushbutton on at once
Increasing thrust and climbing

explanation: Hypoxia is the first danger. The crew puts on their masks and begins the descent to an altitude where the cabin altitude no longer matters.

question: How does the DITCHING pushbutton affect the outflow valve?

options.text: It drives the outflow valve fully open
It transfers control to the manual motor
It closes the outflow valve
It has no effect on the outflow valve

explanation: A closed outflow valve means the water cannot enter through the valve opening during a ditching.

question: How is the aircraft pressurised in flight, in simple terms?

options.text: Air supplied by the packs fills the cabin faster than the outflow valve lets it escape, so the cabin pressure rises above ambient
The outflow valve compresses cabin air with an internal compressor
The cargo hold is pressurised separately by a dedicated pump
The engines push air into the cabin through the doors

explanation: The air conditioning flow supplies a constant mass of air. The pressure of the cabin is set by how much the outflow valve restricts the exit.

question: Why does the cabin altitude in cruise stay well below the aircraft's flight level?

options.text: The system maintains a cabin pressure above ambient, within the structural ΔP limit
Because the cabin is heated
Because the pack flow is increased
Because the outflow valve is closed completely

explanation: At FL390 the cabin altitude is typically around 7 000–8 000 ft, which requires about 8 psi of ΔP.
